EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“External Returns to Education in U.S. States, 1950-1990”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  

Strategy: Two–stage least squares (IV) in a state-of-birth × cohort panel with rich fixed effects (a difference-in-differences flavor).  
• Endogenous variable: Average years of schooling of other workers in an individual’s state of residence and census year (“external schooling”).  
• Instruments: Compulsory-schooling-law (CSL) requirements that applied to the individual’s birth-state cohort—minimum dropout age, minimum years required before leaving school, minimum work-permit age, and minimum schooling for a work permit.  

Why IV is appropriate  
a) External schooling is obviously endogenous: states experiencing positive wage shocks may simultaneously invest more in education.  
b) CSLs preceded labor-market outcomes by 25–50 years, moved discontinuously across states and birth cohorts, and primarily affected schooling attainment. Plausibly exogenous to later wage shocks.  
c) The panel (state-of-birth × birth-cohort × census-year) allows us to difference out fixed state characteristics and common national shocks while exploiting staggered CSL adoption.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
Treated observation = individual exposed to a more restrictive CSL as a child, summarized by an index or the actual CSL components. In the estimating equation the “treatment dose” is the predicted increase in average schooling caused by the CSL.

Control group  
Individuals in the same census year living in states that did not yet (or never) tighten their CSLs for that birth cohort.

Treatment timing  
A CSL change is coded as affecting birth cohort c in state s if the law was in force when cohort c turned 14 (the modal dropout age). Birth-year-specific coding accommodates multiple changes.

Running variable / cutoff  
Not an RDD, so none.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Instrument relevance  
CSLs must raise average schooling. Highly plausible; well documented throughout the high-school movement.

A2. Exclusion (no direct effect)  
Conditional on state, cohort, and census-year fixed effects, CSLs affect adult wages only through their effect on schooling (own and peers’). Plausible because laws were enacted decades earlier and target teenage schooling decisions, not adult labor demand. We will probe with placebo outcomes (e.g., hours worked).  

A3. No differential pre-trends / parallel trends across birth cohorts within states  
Absent CSL changes, cohorts in high-change and low-change states would have followed similar wage trajectories. We will add state-specific linear birth-year trends and perform an event-study plot around law changes.

A4. Stable composition / selective migration is limited  
Use state of birth to assign treatment so migration after school completion does not break identification.

A5. SUTVA across states  
CSL in one state does not directly change wages of another state’s natives (reasonable for this period).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & REMEDIES  

T1  Selective Migration  
People may move to states with higher wages, diluting the “external” measure.  
• Use state of birth × cohort as treatment cell, not state of adult residence.  
• Recompute external schooling leaving out in-migrants (“leave-in-place” definition).  
• Control for own migration dummy in second stage.

T2  Concurrent State-Level Shocks (industry booms, unionization, etc.) correlated with CSL adoption  
• Include state-by-census-year fixed effects, which soak up any time-varying shocks common to all cohorts currently in a state.  
• Add state-specific linear and quadratic birth-year trends.  
• Use falsification tests: run the same IV using pre-law cohorts.

T3  Measurement Error in CSL timing and content  
• Cross-validate CSL dates with multiple historical sources.  
• Use alternative codings (e.g., only minimum dropout age) as robustness.  
• Instrument with each CSL component separately—results should be similar.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)  

```r
# ------------- 0. Packages -------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast FE + IV
library(ivpack)      # weak IV diagnostics
library(tidyverse)

# ------------- 1. Data Loading ----------
ind <- fread("ipums_individuals.csv")            # individual microdata
state_avg <- fread("state_external_school.csv")  # pre-computed leave-one-out averages
csl <- fread("state_csl_history.csv")            # compulsory-schooling-law panel

# ------------- 2. Merge & Variable Construction -------------
# restrict to U.S.-born white men aged 40-49 in 1950–1990 Censuses
ind <- ind[sex=="male" & race=="white" & age%between%c(40,49) & born_us==1]

# log weekly wage
ind[, ln_wage := log(wage_salary_annual/weeks_worked)]

# individual schooling (cap at 17)
ind[, own_yrs_school := pmin(highest_grade_completed, 17)]

# cohort and identifiers
ind[, `:=`(birth_year = year - age,
           cohort      = floor(birth_year/5)*5,           # 5-year bins
           census_year = year)]

# merge state-average schooling (leave individual out)
ind <- merge(ind, state_avg, by = c("state_residence","census_year"), all.x = TRUE)

# merge CSL by state of birth × cohort
csl[, cohort := birth_cohort]                             # already coded to affect cohort at age 14
ind <- merge(ind, csl, by.x = c("state_birth","cohort"), 
             by.y = c("state","cohort"), all.x = TRUE)

# Build a single CSL index (principal component or simple sum)
ind[, csl_index := scale(min_dropout_age) +
                      scale(required_grades_dropout) +
                      scale(min_work_permit_age) +
                      scale(required_grades_work_permit)]

# weights
ind[, wt := person_weight]  # IPUMS person weight

# ------------- 3. First Stage -------------
fs <- feols(state_avg_school ~ csl_index | state_birth + cohort + census_year,
            data = ind, weights = ~wt)
summary(fs)

# ------------- 4. Second Stage -------------
iv <- feols(ln_wage ~ own_yrs_school + state_avg_school | 
              state_birth + cohort + census_year | 
              state_avg_school ~ csl_index,
            data = ind, weights = ~wt, vcov = ~state_birth)
summary(iv)
ivdiag(fs, iv)  # check F-stat & over-ID if multiple instruments

# ------------- 5. Robustness Check -------------
# (i) Include state-specific cohort trends
iv_trend <- feols(ln_wage ~ own_yrs_school + state_avg_school | 
                    state_birth[cohort] + census_year | 
                    state_avg_school ~ csl_index,
                  data = ind, weights = ~wt, vcov = ~state_birth)
summary(iv_trend)

# (ii) Alternative sample: men aged 30–39
alt <- ind[age%between%c(30,39)]
iv_alt <- feols(ln_wage ~ own_yrs_school + state_avg_school | 
                  state_birth + cohort + census_year | 
                  state_avg_school ~ csl_index,
                data = alt, weights = ~wt, vcov = ~state_birth)
summary(iv_alt)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Theory and prior empirical work suggest sizable but smaller “social” than private returns.  
• Private return ~ 7–10 % per additional year of schooling in this period.  
• Anticipated external (peer) effect: 1.5 – 3 % increase in individual wages per additional year of average schooling in one’s state.  
Direction: positive; magnitude likely toward the lower end of private returns but economically meaningful.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV Design)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)

C1. Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) …………………. 1  
C2. Exclusion restriction (no direct CSL → wage path) …. 0.7  
C3. No differential cohort trends within states …………... 0.8  
C4. Limited selective migration / SUTVA ………………... 0.7  
C5. Correct functional form & robust standard errors ….. 1  

Average = 0.84 → reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages plausibly exogenous variation in cohort-specific compulsory schooling laws to identify the causal external wage returns to additional schooling in U.S. states over 1950-1990.
